seo.title: Karmic tail 12 4 10 compatibility: love by imperial decree
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 4 10 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Emperor and The Wheel of Fortune — a union that starts with a pause, lives by rules and learns a rhythm.

title: Karmic tail 12-4-10 in compatibility: the Weaver Girl, the Cowherd and the Heavenly Emperor's decree
short: In a personal destiny matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its two ends, and here that would give 12 + 10 = 22: The Fool, the card of freedom. A couple's middle is counted differently, and in its place sits The Emperor, the card of rules. Tail 12-4-10 tells the story of a love that begins with a pause, passes through a decree and has to learn to live by a rhythm: to come together and drift apart without breaking.

sections.h2: The Weaver Girl and the Cowherd: three layers of one story
paragraphs: On summer nights two bright stars shine on either side of the Milky Way: Vega and Altair. In China they are the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd (literally "the one who leads the ox"), and the Milky Way is the River of Heaven. Out of these three details, over two and a half thousand years, grew a story still celebrated on the seventh evening of the seventh lunar month: Qixi in China, Tanabata in Japan, Chilseok in Korea.

The first layer is the Shijing, the Book of Songs. In the ode "Da Dong" ("The Great East") the people of the eastern lands complain to heaven about the levies, and the stars in it are names that do nothing: "There sprawls the Weaver: seven times a day she changes her station. Seven times she changes — and has woven no pattern. Bright shines the Ox-Leader — and pulls no cart" (our translation). From her very first appearance the Weaver Girl does two things: she goes round with the sky, and she weaves nothing. The wheel and the standstill share one line, long before there is any plot.
The second layer is the Han dynasty "Nineteen Old Poems", the tenth of them. Here the stars are already lovers:

"Far away twinkles the Herd-boy star; / Brightly shines the Lady of the Han River. / Slender, slender she plies her white fingers. / Click, click go the wheels of her spinning-loom. / At the end of the day she has not finished her task; / Her bitter tears fall like streaming rain. / The Han River runs shallow and clear; / Set between them, how short a space! / But the river water will not let them pass, / Gazing at each other but never able to speak" (translated by Arthur Waley).
Waley, who made this translation in 1918, heard wheels in the clatter: the Chinese has only the sound of the shuttle, zha-zha, and the loom. In his English the Weaver Girl's loom turns.

The third layer is the prose plot. In Yin Yun's collection "Xiaoshuo" ("Minor Tales", 6th century; the text survives in later quotations) it fits into a few sentences: "East of the River of Heaven lived the Weaver Girl, daughter of the Heavenly Emperor. Year after year she toiled at the loom, weaving cloud brocade and heavenly robes, with no time to tend to herself. The Emperor took pity on her solitude and let her marry the Cowherd from the western bank. Once married, she gave up weaving. The Emperor grew angry, ordered her back to the eastern bank and allowed them to meet once a year" (our translation).

The bridge came later: on the seventh evening magpies gather over the River and lie down under the couple's feet. In folk versions the river is drawn with a hairpin by the Queen Mother of the West, and the Cowherd takes the bathing Weaver Girl's clothes from the bank, so her sisters fly away without her.

Lay the legend beside the tail and the acts line up with the cards. Solitude, and a marriage for which the loom is abandoned — The Hanged Man. Anger and a decree — The Emperor. A meeting once a year, for which the bridge must be built anew every time — The Wheel. From here on, card by card, with clues from the numbers, the books and the legend itself.

sections.h2: What the 12-4-10 tail is made of: one partner's day and the other's night
paragraphs: Every point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points in two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Running every birth date since 1900 shows that tail 12-4-10 is built from just three combinations of the partners' personal tails.
So in nine couples out of ten, one partner's personal tail runs from The Empress through The Fool to The Sun, while the other's holds The Hermit and The Moon. And they add up like this:

ul: **entry:** one partner's Empress and the other's Hermit — 3 + 9 = 12, The Hanged Man;
**middle:** one partner's Fool and the other's Hermit — 22 + 9 = 31 → 4, The Emperor (in 9% of couples The Fool and The Moon, 22 + 18 = 40 → 4);
**main task:** one partner's Sun and the other's Moon — 19 + 18 = 37 → 10, The Wheel of Fortune (in 9% of couples The Sun and The Hermit, 19 + 9 = 28 → 10).

paragraphs: **Add the Sun to the Moon and you get neither noon nor midnight, but their alternation itself.** In eight couples out of ten the main task is literally made of one partner's day and the other's night. These are numbers, not character traits: a personal tail is read by its own rules and does not make anyone a "sunny" person. But the pattern is the legend's: solitude meets earthly abundance, freedom and solitude produce a rule, day and night produce a wheel.

The remaining 10% are couples in which both partners have the same personal tail, 6-20-14: The Lovers, Judgement, Temperance. The example below belongs here — two people born on the same day. Each of them has The Wheel of Fortune in the centre of their personal chart. What each carries inside alone becomes the couple's main task.

sections.h2: The Hanged Man at the entry: a marriage of heaven and earth that stops the loom
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the entry to the task is the point of the couple's shared wishes and agreements, their "common language". On the site the same point also appears in the "Relationship and common language" sphere. The couple enters the task through this wish, and the same wish can turn into resistance to the task.

In Japan, at Tanabata, people write their wishes on strips of paper and hang them from bamboo. The shared wishes of a 12-4-10 couple are hung up too: until the meeting, until the right moment, until someone's permission.

Waite refuses to reduce The Hanged Man to martyrdom or duty, and speaks of the card with unusual directness: it "expresses the relation, in one of its aspects, between the Divine and the Universe". Heaven and earth, joined in one figure. The Weaver Girl's marriage is exactly that: a heavenly craftswoman and a herdsman from the earthly bank. The numbers show the same meeting: in nine couples out of ten the entry adds The Empress, the card of earthly abundance and home, to The Hermit, the card of solitude on a height.

The pause in the legend runs both ways. Before the marriage the Weaver Girl sits alone at her loom for years, and the Emperor pities her solitude. After it she gives up weaving altogether. **The Hanged Man hangs in both directions: first life without love, then love without life.** The Han poet caught this standstill in two lines: "At the end of the day she has not finished her task" and "Gazing at each other but never able to speak".

Lisovskaya says the same about the twelfth energy in a couple, in everyday words: these two take a long time to enter a relationship, and to marry they often need a push from outside. In the legend the push comes from the Emperor. In life it looks like this: two people have known each other for four years, they go to concerts together, rescue each other through house moves, and friends have long been asking "so when?". The proposal comes the week one of them reaches the end of a lease. Feeling did not decide it — there had been enough of that for ages — circumstances did.

The second pause comes inside the union. For the first six months after the wedding the couple vanishes: phones go quiet, the swimming-pool pass expires unused, the dissertation sits on the shelf. Friends joke that the two have "gone into hibernation". **Both have abandoned their looms — and at first it feels like happiness.** Their common language is soft and generous: "I'll wait", "I'll put it off for us", "whatever suits you". What comes hard is something else: "I need" and "no". This is exactly what Lisovskaya lists in the minus of this energy: no shared goals, no boundaries, nobody able to refuse.

In the plus, The Hanged Man at the entry is a couple that knows how to wait and how to listen. One calls at the very moment the other is struggling, though nothing was said. Both are tactful and attentive and do not rush each other. But a pause has a law the Weaver Girl knew well: whatever has been stopped, sooner or later someone starts putting in order.

sections.h2: The Emperor in the middle: where The Fool was expected, a decree stands
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the task has no meaning of its own — it is an "addition" to the main task. Our reading: the middle shows how the couple travels from its shared wish to its main task, what it does and what it goes through.

By the personal formula The Fool would stand here — the card of the blank page and the step into the unknown. **The couple passes not through freedom but through order.** And The Fool has not gone anywhere: in nine couples out of ten he stands in the middle of one partner's personal tail. Added to the other partner's Hermit or Moon, he sits down on a throne. One partner's freedom plus the other's solitude makes a rule.

In the legend the middle is anger. The Emperor "grew angry, ordered her back to the eastern bank and allowed them to meet once a year". The pause ends not in a conversation but in a decree. Couples know this too: when everything has been stopped for love, someone is first to bring in order, and the order turns out stricter than either of them wanted.

Waite's divinatory list for The Emperor opens with "Stability, power, protection, realization" and closes with "authority and will". Wen writes: "Structure and regulation are pertinent themes." Lisovskaya sees in a couple's four plans, order and rules, and in the minus rigid control, decisions made for everyone and a struggle for leadership. Among the tasks of such a couple she lists one point that might have been copied from the legend: do not create rules that get in the way later.

A year after that hibernation every evening is booked in the shared calendar: Tuesday is the gym, Thursday is the parents, Saturday from seven is "time for us". No one remembers who came up with it, but breaking it feels frightening: the rule looks like care. One partner keeps the budget and decides for both where to go on holiday — "it's safer that way". The other agrees because it is calmer that way, and one day notices that they have not made a single decision at home for a long time. Sometimes the emperor is external: rotation work, two months on and two months off, holidays that must be booked a year ahead, parents who "know better".

The Han poet has a line that exposes all of this: "The Han River runs shallow and clear; / Set between them, how short a space!" The river is shallow. It could be waded; what holds them back is not depth but a ban. **For a 12-4-10 couple the distance is usually not in miles but in a rule:** the only thing stopping a Wednesday meeting is the agreement that Wednesdays are not for that.
If the rules in a couple rest on fear, threats or force, this is no longer the language of the cards. That calls for a psychologist's help, and in danger, a call to a local emergency number.

But The Emperor has another face, and it too can be seen in the Chinese sky. The Heavenly Emperor's palace is the Purple Forbidden Enclosure around the celestial pole; the Forbidden City in Beijing takes its name from it. Confucius compared the ruler who governs by virtue to the pole star: "He who exercises government by means of his virtue may be compared to the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it" (Analects II.1, translated by James Legge). The Emperor of heaven does not only lock the River. He is the axis around which the whole sky turns — the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd included.

The tail has the same geometry: the middle of the task is the axis of the main task. **A rule in this couple can become a river between two banks or the axle of a wheel.** Which it becomes decides how the couple goes through its main task.

sections.h2: The Wheel of Fortune: the main task is to turn a decree into a rhythm
paragraphs: Lisovskaya reads a couple's main task mostly through the minus: what is not working and what the couple has to learn. Her key to the tenth energy is cyclicity: rises and crises in the couple follow one another, and the change itself is to be accepted rather than fought. The hardest thing for this couple is not to treat every downturn as the end.

Waite describes the card as "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and ... the flux of human life". Wen adds an image precise enough for mathematics: "The wheel depicted in the card is also reminiscent of the mathematical concept of the unit circle. The unit circle can further be expressed with periodic functions (e.g., sine or cosine), revealing the philosophy of oscillations between zeniths and nadirs, highs and lows." Plot a 12-4-10 couple's closeness over time and you get exactly that: a sine wave.

In the legend the wheel is the year. Once a year the magpies build the bridge, and they build it from scratch: in Korea people say that after Chilseok magpies and crows have bald heads, because two people walked across them. **Here the bridge is not a structure but an act that has to be repeated.**

The minus of the main task is living only for "seventh evenings". A holiday once a year, a family celebration at the parents', a rare trip — and in between, weekdays in which the two hardly meet. Lisovskaya describes it as a swing between silence and conflict: a month of quiet, a fight over nothing, a stormy reconciliation, quiet again. Each time the Heavenly Emperor is to blame — work, family, fate — or the partner. The Saturday date runs to schedule, but no one actually meets on it.

The best-known lines about the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd were written by the Song poet Qin Guan in "Immortals at the Magpie Bridge": "One meeting of the golden wind and the jade dew outweighs countless meetings in the human world… If the love of two is to last, why must they be together every morning and every evening?" (our translation). The line can be read in two voices. In the Emperor's voice it justifies the decree: there is no need to meet, the rule is fine. In the Wheel's voice it tells the truth: closeness breathes, it waxes and wanes, and lasting love is not the same as being there every day. Which voice speaks depends on one thing — who turns the wheel: the decree, or the two.

Du Fu was sceptical about the legend. "For ten thousand ages they have gazed at each other," he wrote, "but who has seen them together on the seventh evening?" (our translation). Astronomy is on his side: Vega and Altair draw no closer on any night. The meeting exists only as long as it is told — and built. A couple works the same way: the return does not arrive by itself on the appointed day; it is made.

And the sky has a wheel larger than the year. The Earth's axis slowly traces a circle over 26 thousand years, and the celestial pole wanders among the stars. Around 12,000 BCE Vega was the pole star, and around the year 14,000 it will be again. **The Weaver Girl herself will take the Emperor's seat.** For a couple this is the most precise reading of the main task: the throne rotates. Whoever writes the rules today lives by the other's rules tomorrow, and the wheel runs smoothly as long as no one welds themselves to the axle.

In the plus, The Wheel is a couple that changes cities, jobs and roles without losing each other. In the year one of them writes a book or starts a business, the other holds the home; the next year it is the other way round. They can leave and come back without drama, and on returning they ask "what has changed for you?" instead of presenting a bill for the separation. A downturn for them is a phase, not a verdict.

sections.h2: Judgement in the centre and The Lovers in the values: who really writes the decree
paragraphs: The tail is not the only thing these couples share. In 91.4% of them the centre of the matrix — the atmosphere inside the couple — holds Judgement (20); in the remaining 8.6% it holds Strength (11).

Lisovskaya links Judgement in a couple to lineage and family: relatives, traditions, the influence of parents. In the minus: a union made with the approval or through the mediation of relatives, and a partner who decides nothing in their own family without their parents. Once again the legend is precise: the Emperor is the bride's father. He arranged the marriage out of pity and annulled it himself. In folk versions the river is drawn with a hairpin by the Queen Mother of the West, the eldest of the family. **The decree is often written not by the two but by their families — and the couple carries it out as its own.** The relatives sit invisibly at the table: "but Mum said", "that's not how we do things in our family".

Waite describes Judgement as a summons at which the dead rise — a man, a woman and their child — and specifies that this is an answer to "the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within". Waite's divinatory list for Judgement opens with "Change of position, renewal". The difference between a decree and a summons is direction: a decree comes from outside and fixes a position; a summons sounds from within and changes it.
Strength in the centre of the other couples is the same plot in another key: tension that can be tamed by gentleness, or an argument over who tames whom.

In the couple's values, 81.1% of these couples have The Lovers and 18.9% have The Devil. The legend happens to have two versions of its beginning. In the literary one the marriage is made openly, with a blessing. In the folk one the Cowherd takes the Weaver Girl's clothes from the bank, and she can no longer fly away. These are two ways of being together — to choose and to hold. The Lovers is a choice made by two. The Devil is the wish to hold on by hiding the other's wings; Lisovskaya sums up this energy with the words "no one belongs to anyone". Waite's divinatory list for The Lovers includes "trials overcome", while The Hanged Man at the entry has simply "trials". This couple's values begin where the pause ends: a trial passed together.

sections.h2: What Waite's cards show: two wanderers sit down on a throne
paragraphs: The Rider–Waite–Smith pictures add one more clue to this tail. In almost all of these couples the middle is made of The Fool and The Hermit. On Waite's cards both stand on heights, and both hold a staff (The Fool's has a bag hanging from it). The Fool is frozen at the edge of a cliff, and Waite remarks: "His act of eager walking is still indicated, though he is stationary at the given moment." The Hermit holds up his lantern on an eminence, and "It is a star which shines in the lantern."

Added together, the two wanderers sit down on a throne. Waite's Emperor is enthroned with sceptre and orb, and "He is occasionally represented as seated on a cubic stone". The entry to the task is The Hanged Man: a man head down, tied by one ankle, arms behind his back. Two motionless figures, one bound and one seated, stand in the tail before a card on which everything moves.

sections.h2: How the 12-4-10 couple tail is calculated: an example on a single date
paragraphs: Take a couple in which both partners were born on 08.01.1976 (8 January 1976). Each has: day 8, month 1, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task 8 + 1 + 5 = 14, centre 8 + 1 + 5 + 14 = 28 → 10. Tail entry 14 + 10 = 24 → 6, middle 6 + 14 = 20: personal tail 6-20-14, with The Wheel of Fortune in the centre. The couple's tail is added point by point:
The couple's centre is 10 + 10 = 20, Judgement. In this couple's values stands The Devil (15): it belongs to the 18.9%.

A couple's middle is not recalculated from the ends: it is added from the partners' middles. Otherwise 12 + 10 would give 22, The Fool. In a personal matrix this tail is impossible altogether: there the entry equals the main task plus the centre, and to get an entry of 12 with a main task of 10 you would need a centre of 2 — and no person has such a centre. Tail 12-4-10 is born only between two people.

There are no couple tails made of the same numbers. A couple's entry is always a multiple of three (3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21), so 4 and 10 cannot come first, and the order 12-10-4 does not occur for any couple. The tail itself is rare: it falls to roughly one couple in 911 (0.11%) and ranks 80th of the 97 couple tails.

sections.h2: The strong version of tail 12-4-10: how a couple turns the wheel itself
paragraphs: A strong couple with this tail does not abolish the pause or the rules. It changes what they are for: the pause becomes a breather, the rule an axle, the separation a phase.

ul: **Name the decree out loud.** Write down the rules the couple lives by and, next to each, who wrote it: both, one, work or family. A rule with no author is usually the one that gets in the way most.
**Check: river or axle?** A river-rule pushes the banks apart: "we don't see each other on weekdays". An axle-rule keeps the turning going: "after every hard month, a day just for us".
**Give each their own loom back.** Each should keep their own work, their own people, their own time. A love for which everything was dropped turns into a pause, and a pause calls for the Emperor.
**Plan the returns, not the separations.** What goes in the calendar is not "a meeting once a week" but how the couple will come back to each other after busy weeks.
**Pass the throne.** In different matters and different seasons, first one and then the other takes charge. The Weaver Girl will one day take the pole star's place — the wheel allows for it.
**Don't take the Heavenly Emperor to court.** In a downturn, look for a culprit neither in fate nor in each other; ask what phase this is and what it needs.
**Build the bridge every time.** A meeting has a ritual made by hand: a walk, a conversation without phones, a shared breakfast. The magpies do not wait for the bridge to build itself.

paragraphs: In China Qixi is not only a lovers' festival. In the 6th century Zong Lin recorded in his "Jingchu Suishiji" ("Record of the Seasons of Jingchu") that on the night when the Weaver Girl meets the Cowherd, women tie coloured threads, pass them through needles with seven eyes and set out melons and fruit in the courtyard, "begging for skill". If a spider spins a web over a melon, it is a good sign. **The festival of love turned out to be a festival of craft: on the night of the meeting, people ask the Weaver Girl for deft hands.** What the decree divided — the loom and the meeting — the festival joined. That is the strong version of tail 12-4-10: love and work turn in one wheel, and the two of them turn it.

ul: **Entry to the task — The Hanged Man (12).** The couple's common language is the pause. These two linger on the threshold of a union for a long time, and once inside it they are ready to stop the rest of life for each other.
**Middle of the task — The Emperor (4).** The path runs through rules: routines, roles, decisions made for both. The couple writes the decree itself or accepts one from work, family or circumstance.

**Main task — The Wheel of Fortune (10).** Closeness in this couple waxes and wanes in waves. What it has to learn is rhythm: not to freeze the relationship and not to govern it by decree, but to turn the wheel together.

intro: This plot was written down long ago. The Chinese legend of the Weaver Girl and the Cowherd is one of the oldest love stories there is: the Heavenly Emperor gave the Weaver Girl in marriage, then divided the couple by a river and let them meet once a year. The legend's three acts come in the order of the three cards. There is no prophecy of separation here: the legend shows the mechanism by which a couple turns love into a timetable — and can turn the timetable back into love.

faq.q: What does karmic tail 12-4-10 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the story of a couple that enters a union through a pause (The Hanged Man), passes through rules and routine (The Emperor) and learns rhythm — the rises and falls of closeness, changes and returns (The Wheel of Fortune). The main task is not to replace a living rhythm with a decree and not to freeze the relationship.

No. The cards do not predict events. The legend of a meeting once a year shows a mechanism: a couple can itself turn love into a timetable. The tail's task is to make the rhythm its own and the rule an axle, not a river between two banks.

faq.q: Why is The Emperor in the middle if 12 + 10 = 22?
faq.a: The middle is calculated from the ends only in a personal matrix. In a couple every point is added from the partners' matching points: in 81% of these couples it is one partner's Fool and the other's Hermit, 22 + 9 = 31 → 4. Where the personal formula would put The Fool, the couple has The Emperor.

faq.q: Does tail 12-4-10 occur in a personal destiny matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the tail's entry equals the main task plus the centre, and an entry of 12 with a main task of 10 would need a centre of 2, which no person has. Tail 12-4-10 appears only in a couple's matrix, in roughly one couple in 911.

faq.q: Are there couple tails made of the same numbers?
faq.a: No. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, so 4 and 10 cannot come first, and the order 12-10-4 does not occur for any couple. The triple 12-4-10 is the only one.

report: Add up the ends of tail 12-4-10 the way it is done in a personal matrix, and the middle would come out as The Fool: 12 + 10 = 22, the card of freedom and the step into the unknown. But a couple's middle is added from the middles of two people, and in that place sits The Emperor, the card of rules. Where a single person would find freedom, the couple finds a decree.

unit.meaning: Your love slips into pauses and timetables; the task is to make the rule the axle of your rhythm, not a river between you.
